title: Microsoft made $10B from OpenAI deals in a single quarter
content:
Microsoft generated $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, in the quarter ended September 30, the company said in a regulatory filing on Wednesday. That represents nearly 11% of Microsoft’s total quarterly revenue of $92.3 billion, highlighting the enormous financial ties that remain between the two companies even as they increasingly compete for the same customers.
(Microsoft’s financial year begins in July, making the quarter ended September 30, 2026 the first quarter of its fiscal 2027.)
For the full 2026 fiscal year, revenue from OpenAI hit $24.1 billion. At its latest quarterly pace, Microsoft would pull in $40 billion annually from OpenAI-related arrangements.
Microsoft also reported $7.2 billion in outstanding receivables from OpenAI at the end of September, up from $6 billion at the end of June. That money represents amounts OpenAI owes for previous transactions, not additional revenue.
It’s not clear how much of Microsoft’s revenue from OpenAI came from revenue-sharing payments or Azure cloud computing services. TechCrunch has reached out for more information. In November 2025, TechCrunch reported, citing leaked documents, that Microsoft had received $865.8 million in net revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI during the first nine months of that year.
OpenAI reportedly shares 20% of its revenue with Microsoft as part of a previous deal in which the software giant invested more than $13 billion in the AI startup. (Neither the AI lab nor Microsoft have publicly confirmed this percentage.) As part of an April 2026 agreement, OpenAI is on the hook to continue sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030, subject to a cap, even as OpenAI is allowed to work with competing cloud providers.
The companies began loosening the ties of their once-exclusive partnership in October 2025, when Microsoft relinquished its hold on OpenAI to give the startup more freedom to partner with other cloud providers. In exchange, OpenAI committed to buying an additional $250 billion in Azure services as part of an October 2025 agreement.
Microsoft’s ownership stake in OpenAI has also declined slightly from about 25% in June to 24% in September. That continues a gradual decline from roughly 27% following the October 2025 recapitalization. Microsoft did not specify what caused the dilution.

report.summary: Microsoft earned $10B from OpenAI commercial arrangements in the quarter ended Sept. 30, nearly 11% of its $92.3B revenue.
report.background: Microsoft’s financial relationship with OpenAI dates to a multi-billion-dollar investment and a deal that made Azure the AI lab’s preferred cloud. The partnership helped Microsoft become an early enterprise gateway to generative AI while giving OpenAI compute and capital. As OpenAI’s ambitions grew, the companies renegotiated: in October 2025 Microsoft gave up exclusivity, and OpenAI committed to buy $250 billion in Azure services. An April 2026 agreement extended revenue sharing through 2030, subject to a cap, even as OpenAI could use rival clouds. Microsoft’s equity stake has also been diluted. The new filing shows how much Microsoft still depends on OpenAI-related revenue even as the two firms compete for customers.
key_points: Microsoft booked $10 billion from OpenAI commercial arrangements in the quarter ended Sept. 30, about 11% of its $92.3 billion total revenue. At that quarterly pace, the OpenAI-related line would run at roughly $40 billion a year. For fiscal 2026, Microsoft reported $24.1 billion from OpenAI.

The filing does not split how much came from OpenAI revenue-sharing payments versus Azure cloud services. Microsoft also reported $7.2 billion in outstanding receivables from OpenAI, up from $6 billion at the end of June. Those receivables are money owed for past transactions, not new revenue.

The partnership is no longer exclusive. Under an October 2025 deal, Microsoft loosened its cloud hold and OpenAI committed to buy an additional $250 billion in Azure services. An April 2026 agreement keeps OpenAI sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030, subject to a cap, while allowing OpenAI to work with competing cloud providers.

Microsoft’s stake in OpenAI slipped to about 24% in September from roughly 25% in June, continuing a decline from about 27% after the October 2025 recapitalization. Microsoft did not explain the dilution. The changing ownership and capped revenue share suggest the financial ties are being gradually reshaped even as they remain enormous.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the numbers show that the cloud-AI lab alliance is still a major profit engine—and a concentration risk. Microsoft’s results may face scrutiny over how much OpenAI revenue is high-margin sharing versus lower-margin Azure compute. For developers, the restructuring preserves OpenAI access on Azure but opens more multi-cloud options, which could improve choice and pricing over time; near term, capacity and API costs still depend on these giants. For regular users, the money flowing between Microsoft and OpenAI funds model development and product integration, but it also reinforces bundled ecosystems and raises questions about whether AI subscription prices reflect real costs or cross-subsidy.
report.tools: To follow the money, watch Microsoft Investor Relations and SEC EDGAR filings for segment detail; TechCrunch’s ongoing coverage for OpenAI deal terms; and OpenAI and Microsoft Azure documentation for product and pricing changes. For open-source analysis, use OpenBB for financial data, edgartools for parsing SEC filings, and Crunchbase-style databases or Wikidata for ownership tracking.
